title: Designing a self-funded "cash machine": 150 customers, high prices, annual prepay
summary: Jason Cohen lays out his model for a bootstrapped business: aim for predictable recurring revenue of $10k/month per founder from about 150 customers at roughly $70 each. He covers raising prices, annual prepay for cash flow, B2B markets with naturally recurring pain, and paid acquisition over social media.

principles.text: Design for a cash machine: predictable recurring revenue of $10k/month per founder, built on about 150 customers at ~$70/month rather than 1,000 fans.
principles.quote: something that predictably and repeatedly always gives you $10,000 a month per founder in revenue and hopefully more like 20 30 40

principles.text: Raise prices far more aggressively than feels comfortable. Doubling price often leaves signups unchanged, and low prices force you to find thousands of customers.
principles.quote: they doubled it to 49 or whatever it was and signups didn't change at all

principles.text: Push annual prepay so each customer's cash arrives upfront. This lets you out-spend acquisition cost and run marketing with no money constraint.
principles.quote: we literally operate with an infinite marketing budget the marketing budget at W engine is not limited by money because we'll make it back

principles.text: Replace free trials with a long money-back guarantee. You collect cash up front, customers get more time, and signups and customer counts went up.
principles.quote: we switched to a 60-day money-back guarantee instead of a 15-day free trial

principles.text: Sell B2B, not to consumers, because consumers won't pay meaningful monthly prices. Favor markets where the pain or cost is naturally recurring, not temporary.
principles.quote: I want to make a very strong argument that you should absolutely never not not not sell to consumers people don't spend money on stuff

principles.text: Prefer paid acquisition you can model over social media. Use a rule of thumb for what you can pay per click: average revenue per customer divided by 25.
principles.quote: you take how much average revenue you get per customer divided by 25 and that's what you can pay per click
